mcqs.question: A framework draws every pixel itself using its own rendering engine, bypassing the OS's native widget toolkit entirely. Which strategy is this?
options: Self-rendered
Fully native
Hybrid-native
There is no such strategy — every framework must use the OS's widgets
mcqs.explanation: Self-rendered describes exactly this: the framework owns its own engine and draws pixels directly, which is Flutter's approach. Fully native means compiling to actual platform widgets on each OS, and hybrid-native means a shared logic layer drives real native components — neither bypasses the OS widget toolkit the way self-rendered does.

mcqs.question: A Flutter app looks visually identical on iOS and Android without any platform-specific styling. What's the trade-off this implies?
options: It will crash on one of the two platforms since Flutter can't run identical widgets cross-platform
It automatically becomes platform-idiomatic on both operating systems
It will feel slightly foreign on at least one platform, since matching each OS's real conventions requires deliberately using platform-adaptive widgets
It has no trade-off — pixel-identical rendering is a pure win with no downside
mcqs.explanation: Pixel-identical rendering is a direct consequence of Flutter drawing everything itself rather than asking each OS for its native-styled widgets, so without deliberately using Cupertino or platform-adaptive components, the app won't automatically match either OS's real conventions. It doesn't crash, and it isn't automatically idiomatic on both — that requires explicit platform branching.

mcqs.question: What was Impeller specifically introduced to address in Flutter's rendering pipeline?
options: The bridge serialization overhead between JavaScript and native code
Runtime shader compilation jank on first paint of certain effects, by precompiling shaders ahead of time
The lack of platform-specific styling in Flutter's default widget set
Slow app startup time caused by the Dart virtual machine
mcqs.explanation: Impeller replaces Skia specifically to fix jank from compiling shaders at runtime on first use — it precompiles them ahead of time instead. The bridge/serialization issue is a React Native concept, not a Flutter rendering engine issue, and Impeller isn't about widget styling or Dart VM startup.

mcqs.question: Why does a drag gesture that fires many small position updates per frame risk visible lag under React Native's classic bridge architecture?
options: JavaScript itself cannot process touch events fast enough on any architecture
The bridge only supports one message per second by hard limit
Native views cannot receive more than one update per second
Each update crossing the bridge pays a serialize/queue/deserialize cost, and many small individual round-trips per frame can add up to visible lag if not batched
mcqs.explanation: The bridge's cost comes from serializing and queuing every cross-boundary message, not from JavaScript execution speed itself — a high-frequency stream of small individual updates pays that tax repeatedly unless batched. There's no fixed one-message-per-second bridge limit or native view update cap.

mcqs.question: What does JSI fundamentally change about how JavaScript communicates with native code in React Native's New Architecture?
options: It removes JavaScript from the app entirely, replacing it with native Swift/Kotlin code
It allows JavaScript to hold direct references to native objects and call methods synchronously, without the async bridge's serialization and queuing
It moves all UI rendering onto a GPU-only rendering engine similar to Flutter's
It requires every native module to be rewritten in TypeScript
mcqs.explanation: JSI's core change is enabling synchronous, direct calls between JavaScript and native C++ objects, eliminating the async bridge's serialize/queue/deserialize overhead. It doesn't remove JavaScript, switch to a GPU-only engine like Flutter's, or require rewriting native modules in TypeScript.

mcqs.question: A team plans a cross-platform app assuming 100% of the code will be shared between iOS and Android. What commonly goes wrong?
options: Nothing — modern cross-platform frameworks genuinely achieve 100% shared code with zero exceptions
The app fails to compile on one platform entirely
They underestimate a realistic platform-specific slice — push notification setup, certain permissions, deep OS integrations — and scramble near ship date
The shared codebase becomes twice as large as either native codebase would have been
mcqs.explanation: Real cross-platform apps still need platform-specific code for things frameworks don't fully abstract — push registration flows, certain permission dialogs, deep platform integrations — and teams that plan for zero platform-specific work consistently get surprised by this near release. It doesn't cause a compile failure or double the codebase size by itself.
